analysis.one_liner: Bars pesticide residues on food unless health risk is negligible, with special protections for children.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after one subcommittee hearing, it died in committee when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten how the government sets legal limits for pesticide residues on food. Any residue without an approved limit would be treated as unsafe, and a limit could only be set if the health risk from a lifetime of eating the food — including exposure from drinking water — was negligible. It required special safety analysis for infants and young children, mandated retesting of every existing tolerance (many dating back decades), and charged pesticide makers fees to fund the reviews. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and never came up for a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats food grown with pesticides — most of the population — would get stronger legal protection against residues, with explicit risk analysis for babies and young children and for combined exposure from food and drinking water. Any person, not just industry, could petition to revoke an unsafe tolerance and could sue to enforce the standards, with attorney fees available to winners.

how_it_helps.text: Any pesticide residue not covered by an approved tolerance or exemption would be deemed unsafe and make the food adulterated, closing gaps in existing law [S2] [S3].
A tolerance could only be set if dietary risk over a lifetime was negligible, counted from all sources including drinking water, not just the crop being regulated [S2] [S3].
The risk analysis had to cover infants, children at every age from 1 to 10, adolescents, and other sensitive groups separately [S3].
EPA had to re-evaluate every existing tolerance within set deadlines — 30% of them within 2 years and 100% within 7 years — and revoke or lower any that failed the health standard [S2] [S3].
No tolerance could stay in effect unless there was a practical method for the government to actually detect the residue in routine food testing [S2] [S3].
Any person — including someone with no financial stake — could petition to establish, lower, or revoke a tolerance, and could seek court review with attorney fees if they won [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers, who would pay fees to fund EPA's reviews and could lose products whose tolerances were revoked; farmers and food processors, who could lose crop-protection tools and face tighter residue limits on processed foods; and consumers, who would likely pay somewhat more for food as restricted chemicals raised production costs.

drawbacks.text: The health-only 'negligible risk' standard gave regulators no room to weigh the farm value of a pesticide, so many useful crop-protection chemicals could have been banned outright, raising costs for growers and food prices for shoppers [S3].
Any tolerance would be automatically revoked if EPA had not approved a suitable detection method within three years, potentially removing legal residues even where safety was not in doubt [S3].
The bill required fees large enough to fully fund EPA's review work and let continuation of a tolerance be conditioned on annual fee payment — costs registrants would pass along [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health gain was substantial: existing tolerances had never been systematically retested against a modern health standard, and the bill would have forced that reckoning with children's exposure counted separately. The cost was real but manageable — tighter residue limits mean some chemicals come off the market and food costs rise modestly — and the bill deliberately excluded cost-benefit balancing, which was the core argument against it. A reasonable observer could support the health goal while faulting the rigid mechanics.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's health subcommittee, got a single hearing in June 1991, and died when the Congress ended without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on May 14, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on May 24, 1991, and the subcommittee held hearings on June 19, 1991 [S5].
No further action was taken: the committee never reported the bill, no floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers and growers were better off: the looser pre-existing rules on residues stayed in place for the rest of the Congress, with no mandatory retesting of old tolerances and no new fees. Consumers continued eating food regulated under limits that had never been verified against a modern health standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide makers and their farm customers

for.name: Henry Waxman
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA); Chair, Health and Environment Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and got it a hearing in the health subcommittee he chaired; no markup or floor vote followed.

for.name: 3 House cosponsors (2 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it small bipartisan sponsorship but little visible backing.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill, never scheduled a markup, and never reported it to the floor.

against.name: Pesticide manufacturers and agricultural groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed replacing the existing residue rules with a strict negligible-risk standard that could ban chemicals still in wide use.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four sponsors included two Democrats and one Republican, but with only one hearing and no votes, the record shows no partisan split on the outcome.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed fees funding EPA reviews, forced retesting of every tolerance, and required revocation of any tolerance failing a negligible-risk standard — likely removing chemicals from the market. Its interest in the bill ran against consumers' interest in lower residue exposure.
Revoked or lowered tolerances would have restricted crop-protection tools and raised production costs. Growers' stake in keeping chemicals available ran against the consumer safety benefit.
The bill required processed-food residue limits set at the lowest level achievable under good manufacturing practice, tightening standards for packaged and processed foods.
